title: Yet they hold this leaves contingency intact: God decreed not only the event but its free mode
source_text: VIII. Quanquam autem Deus, ex eorum mente, aeterno suo decreto praedeterminaverit & praedefinierit quaecunque in tempore a causis quibuslibet fiunt, istud nihil obstare pertendunt quominus multa non necessario, sed contingenter & libere fiant: quoniam aeterna Dei providentia non omnibus eventibus & effectibus praeparavit causas necessarias, sed quibusdam causas liberas, sive contingentes; neque solum determinavit hoc vel illud fieri, sed etiam modum quo res quaeque fieret, adeoque voluit ut quaedam necessario, alia vero contingenter & libere fierent. Et sic tantum abest ut aeterna Dei Providentia libertatem tollat actuum humanorum, ut contra quicquid est in rebus libertatis & contingentiae ad ipsum tanquam ad causam primam referendum sit: quia, scilicet, Deus non tantum res esse voluit, sed etiam voluntate sua statuit & definivit modum & rationem quo singulae esse deberent.
pass_a_gloss: VIII. But although God, according to their mind, has by his eternal decree predetermined and predefined whatever things are done in time by any causes, they contend that this does not at all hinder many things from being done not necessarily, but contingently and freely: since the eternal providence of God has not prepared necessary causes for all events and effects, but for some free or contingent causes; and has not only determined that this or that be done, but also the mode in which each thing should be done, and so willed that some things be done necessarily, but others contingently and freely. And thus so far is it from being the case that the eternal Providence of God takes away the freedom of human acts, that on the contrary whatever there is of freedom and contingency in things is to be referred to him as to the first cause: because, namely, God not only willed things to be, but also by his will established and defined the mode and manner in which each ought to be.
pass_b_english: On their view, God by his eternal decree predetermined and predefined whatever is done in time by any cause. Even so, they maintain that nothing prevents many things from happening not by necessity but contingently and freely.

God's eternal providence did not provide necessary causes for every event and effect; for some it provided free or contingent causes. Nor did it determine only that this or that should happen; it also determined the way each thing should happen. So God willed some things to happen necessarily, and others contingently and freely.

Far from removing the freedom of human acts, then, God's eternal providence is the first cause to which whatever freedom and contingency there is in things must be traced. For God willed not only that things should be, but also by his will settled and defined the mode and manner in which each should be.

choices.why: God's fixing an act beforehand by decree; 'predefine' keeps the Schools' term distinct from predetermination, and 'foreordain' renders praefinire where the authors use it as a synonym.
